title: Logical Thinking
description: Read if-then statements correctly, spot arguments that don't hold up, and crack deduction puzzles.
keyIdeas: A statement is true or false. NOT, AND and OR combine statements, and a truth table checks every case.
'If P then Q' is only broken when P is true and Q is false. Its contrapositive means the same; its converse and inverse don't.
'P only if Q' means 'if P then Q': P is **sufficient** for Q, and Q is **necessary** for P.
Valid means the conclusion can't be false while the premises are true. Watch for affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent.
One counterexample defeats an 'all'. To deny 'some', you need 'none'.
Solve puzzles by elimination: rule things out, chase what's forced, and test assumptions for contradictions.

units.title: Building blocks
units.description: Statements, NOT, AND, OR, and truth tables to check every case.

lessons.title: Your first deduction
lessons.takeaway: A statement is either true or false, NOT flips it, and clues let you rule things out until only one answer is left.

steps.title: A mix-up at the Puzzle Café
steps.body:
Ana, Ben and Cleo meet at the **Puzzle Café** every Friday. Tonight they ordered a latte, a tea and a cocoa, one each, and the new waiter forgot who ordered what.

You don't need to guess. Each clue **rules out** some pairings. Cross those out, and when a person has only one drink left, that's theirs, and nobody else can have it.

steps.prompt: Who ordered which drink? Use the clues to fill in the grid.
clues: Ben doesn't drink coffee, so the latte isn't his.
Ana passed the tea across the table to whoever ordered it.
steps.hint: Start with Ana: two clues are about her. Which drink is left for her?
steps.explanation: Clue 2 means Ana didn't order the tea (she handed it to someone else), and clue 3 rules out the latte, so **Ana has the cocoa**. Clue 1 rules the latte out for Ben, and the cocoa is taken, so **Ben has the tea**. That leaves **Cleo with the latte**. Notice that no clue said who had what directly: every clue was a *not*, and elimination did the rest.

steps.title: Clues are statements
steps.body:
Every clue you just used is a **statement**: a sentence that is either **true** or **false**. Logic doesn't ask whether it sounds convincing, only whether it's true or false.

- 'Ben doesn't drink coffee.' A statement.
- 'Paris is in Spain.' Also a statement, just a false one.
- 'Pass the sugar.' Not a statement: a request can't be true or false.
- 'Is the latte Ana's?' Not a statement: it's a question.

steps.prompt: Can it be true or false? Sort each sentence.

items.text: The café opens at 8 a.m.
The Moon is made of cheese.
There are exactly 31 chairs in the café.
Ben ordered the cocoa or Cleo did.
Please close the door.
Who ordered the tea?
Let's play chess after dinner.
Hooray!

steps.hint: Ask: could someone reply 'That's true' or 'That's false'? A false claim still counts.
steps.explanation: A **statement** makes a claim that is true or false, even if it's false (the Moon) or you can't check it right now (the 31 chairs: someone could count them). 'Ben ordered the cocoa or Cleo did' combines two statements and is still a statement. Requests, questions, suggestions and exclamations don't claim anything, so they can't be true or false.

steps.title: NOT flips it
steps.body:
**NOT** turns a statement into its opposite. If P is true, *not P* is false, and the other way round.

A correct negation is true in **exactly** the cases where the original is false, no more and no less. The negation of 'The coffee is hot' is 'The coffee is **not** hot', which includes lukewarm. 'The coffee is cold' is too strong: it skips the in-between cases.

steps.prompt: What is the negation of **'Ben is taller than Ana'**?
choices: Ana is taller than Ben
Ben is not taller than Ana: Ana is taller, or they're the same height
Ben is shorter than Ana
Ben and Ana are the same height
steps.hint: Imagine Ben and Ana are exactly the same height. Which option is true then?
steps.explanation: The negation must cover **every** case where the original is false. If they're the same height, 'Ben is taller' is false, but 'Ana is taller' and 'Ben is shorter' are false too, so those can't be the negation. Only 'Ben is not taller than Ana' covers both 'shorter' and 'same height'.

steps.prompt: Let P = 'The café is open'. Fill in **not P**, then flip it again.
steps.explanation: NOT swaps T and F. Flip twice and you're back where you started: **not (not P)** has the same value as P in every row. That's why 'It's not true that the café isn't open' simply means the café is open.

steps.prompt: A puzzle clue says: *'It is not true that Cleo didn't order the latte.'* What does it tell you?
choices: Cleo ordered the latte
Cleo didn't order the latte
Nothing: it cancels itself out
Someone other than Cleo ordered the latte
steps.explanation: Two NOTs cancel: *not (not P)* = P. Here P is 'Cleo ordered the latte', so the clue simply says Cleo ordered the latte. Double negatives don't erase a clue; they bring it back to the plain statement.

lessons.title: AND, OR and truth tables
lessons.takeaway: AND needs both parts true, OR needs at least one; to negate either, negate each part and swap AND with OR.

steps.title: Combining statements
steps.body:
**AND** is true only when **both** parts are true. **OR**, in logic, is true when **at least one** part is true, including when both are.

A **truth table** lists every possible combination. With two statements P and Q there are 4 rows: both true (TT), only P (TF), only Q (FT), neither (FF). Fill one in and you've checked every case, with no guessing.

steps.prompt: Friday plans. P = 'Ana brings snacks', Q = 'Ben brings a game'. Fill in when each combination is true.
steps.hint: AND: are both true? OR: is at least one true?
steps.explanation: **AND** is true in one row only: when both happen. **OR** is false in one row only: when neither happens. In the TT row OR is true too: Ana bringing snacks *and* Ben bringing a game certainly satisfies 'snacks or a game'.

steps.prompt: A cinema sign says **'Students or seniors get 10% off.'** Cleo's grandmother, aged 70, is taking a university course, so she's a student *and* a senior. Using logic's OR, does she get the discount?
choices: Yes: OR is true when at least one part is true, and both parts are
No: OR means she has to be exactly one of them
No: she can only claim one reason for the discount
It can't be decided from the sign
steps.explanation: Logic's OR is **inclusive**: it's satisfied by one part *or both*. Being both a student and a senior makes 'student or senior' true. No sensible cinema would refuse her for qualifying twice.

steps.title: When OR means 'one, not both'
steps.body:
Sometimes everyday 'or' means **exactly one**: 'The lunch special comes with soup or salad' usually means you pick one, not both. Logic calls this **exclusive or (XOR)**: true when the parts differ.

When a sentence is ambiguous, ask one question: **is 'both' allowed?**

steps.prompt: Is 'both' allowed? Sort each use of 'or'.

items.text: Students or seniors get 10% off
Bring a pen or a pencil to the exam
You can reach us by email or phone
Free delivery if you spend $20 or you're a member
Heads or tails?
Is the café open or closed right now?
Pick one side: soup or salad comes with the special
Does Friday's game start at 7 or at 8?

steps.hint: Try imagining both parts happening at once. Is that impossible, or not allowed? Then it's exclusive.
steps.explanation: Bringing a pen *and* a pencil, or spending $20 *as* a member, obviously still counts: those are **inclusive**. A coin can't land both ways, a café can't be open and closed at once, a game starts at one time, and 'pick one side' rules out both: those are **exclusive**. In logic, plain OR means inclusive unless you say otherwise.

steps.title: Negating AND and OR
steps.body:
How do you deny 'Ana brings snacks **and** Ben brings a game'? It fails as soon as **either** part fails:

**not (P and Q)** = **(not P) or (not Q)**

And an OR fails only when **both** parts fail:

**not (P or Q)** = **(not P) and (not Q)**

These are **De Morgan's laws**: negate each part, and swap AND with OR.

steps.prompt: Check De Morgan's law yourself. The AND column is filled in for you: fill in the other two and compare them row by row.
steps.hint: For the last column, work out not P and not Q in your head for each row, then OR them.
steps.explanation: Both columns are **F, T, T, T**: false only in the top row, where P and Q are both true. Columns that match in every row are **equivalent**: they say the same thing in different words. So 'not both' means 'at least one of them fails'.

steps.prompt: The forecast says: **'Saturday will be sunny and warm.'** Which statement is true exactly when the forecast is wrong?
choices: Saturday won't be sunny, and it won't be warm
Saturday won't be sunny, or it won't be warm (or both)
Saturday will be cloudy and cold
Saturday will be sunny but not warm
steps.explanation: Negate each part and swap AND for OR. A sunny but chilly day already makes the forecast wrong, so the negation can't require *both* failures. Option 1 is the classic slip: it only covers the worst case. Option 4 is just one of the ways the forecast can fail.

steps.prompt: Ben says: **'Dev drinks coffee or tea.'** What would prove Ben wrong?
choices: Dev drinks neither coffee nor tea
Dev doesn't drink coffee, or he doesn't drink tea
Dev drinks both coffee and tea
Dev drinks tea but not coffee
steps.explanation: not (C or T) = (not C) **and** (not T): an OR claim is only false when **both** parts fail, so Dev must drink neither. If Dev drinks only tea, or both, Ben's claim is still true.

units.title: If-then and arguments
units.description: Read conditionals correctly and tell good arguments from convincing-sounding ones.

lessons.title: If-then, decoded
lessons.takeaway: 'If P then Q' is false only when P is true and Q is false, so to test it, check the P cases and the not-Q cases.

steps.title: A promise with a trigger
steps.body:
The barista says: **'If you finish the puzzle, you get a free cookie.'** Call 'you finish the puzzle' **P** and 'you get a cookie' **Q**.

When is that promise **broken**? Only one way: you finished (P true) and got no cookie (Q false).

If you didn't finish, the promise doesn't say anything, so a cookie or no cookie both leave it unbroken. Logic counts an unbroken if-then as **true**.

steps.prompt: Kept or broken? Sort each outcome.

items.text: Barista: 'If you finish the puzzle, you get a cookie.' You finish and get a cookie.
Barista: 'If you finish the puzzle, you get a cookie.' You give up and get no cookie.
Barista: 'If you finish the puzzle, you get a cookie.' You give up but get a cookie anyway.
Barista: 'If you finish the puzzle, you get a cookie.' You finish and get no cookie.
Cleo: 'If it rains, I'll bring an umbrella.' It's sunny and she brings one anyway.
Cleo: 'If it rains, I'll bring an umbrella.' It rains and she has no umbrella.
Sign: 'If you're under 12, you eat free.' A 40-year-old is charged.
Sign: 'If you're under 12, you eat free.' A 10-year-old is charged.

steps.hint: First ask: did the 'if' part happen? If not, the promise can't have been broken.
steps.explanation: An if-then is broken **only** when the trigger happens (P true) and the promised result doesn't (Q false). A generous barista who hands out a cookie anyway, or Cleo carrying an umbrella on a sunny day, breaks nothing: the rule never said what happens when P is false.

steps.prompt: Now as a truth table. Fill in **P → Q** ('if P then Q') for every row.
steps.explanation: **T, F, T, T.** The only false row is P true, Q false: you finished and got no cookie. The two bottom rows are true because the promise was never triggered. Logicians call these *vacuously* true: 'If you finish, you get a cookie' isn't a lie just because you didn't finish.

steps.prompt: The famous card test. Each card has a letter on one side and a number on the other. Rule: **'If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other.'** You see four cards: **E**, **K**, **4**, **7**. Which cards *must* you turn over to check the rule?
choices: E and 4
E only
E and 7
E, 4 and 7
steps.hint: Look for possible broken promises: which visible faces could be half of a 'vowel + odd number' card?
steps.explanation: The rule is broken only by a card with a **vowel and an odd number**. **E** might have an odd number on the back, and **7** might have a vowel. **4** can't break it: the rule never said even numbers need vowels, so a consonant behind it is fine. **K** isn't a vowel, so it's irrelevant. In Wason's experiments, fewer than 10% of people tended to choose E and 7; 'E and 4' was the most common answer.

steps.prompt: Same logic, friendlier story. Café rule: **'If you take a free refill, you must have a loyalty card.'** You see four customers: one taking a refill, one not taking a refill, one with a loyalty card, and one without. Whose details must you check?
choices: The refill-taker and the person without a card
The refill-taker and the person with a card
Only the refill-taker
All four
steps.explanation: It's the card test in disguise. P = takes a refill, Q = has a card. Check **P** (is the refill-taker carrying a card?) and **not Q** (is the cardless person sneaking a refill?). The card holder can take a refill or not: either way, no rule is broken. People tend to find this version much easier, even though the logic is identical.

steps.title: If-then in disguise
steps.body:
If-then hides in many phrasings. All of these say *if you finish the puzzle, you get a cookie*:

- 'Finish the puzzle **and** you get a cookie.'
- '**Every** puzzle finisher gets a cookie.'
- 'You get a cookie **whenever** you finish.'
- 'You get a cookie **if** you finish.'

Find the trigger (**P**) and the guaranteed result (**Q**). The 'if' part is the trigger, even when it comes second.

steps.prompt: Rule: **'If it's Friday, the café has puzzle night.'** You walk past and see puzzle night in full swing. Can you conclude it's Friday?
choices: Yes: puzzle night means it's Friday
No: the rule doesn't say puzzle night happens *only* on Fridays
No: the rule must be false
Yes, but only if the rule is true
steps.explanation: The rule promises puzzle night on Fridays. It says nothing about other days, so the café might also run one on Tuesdays. Concluding P from Q is a classic mistake called **affirming the consequent**; you'll meet it properly in the arguments lesson.

lessons.title: Converse, inverse, contrapositive
lessons.takeaway: An if-then always means the same as its contrapositive, never automatically its converse or inverse; and 'P only if Q' means 'if P then Q'.

steps.title: Four look-alikes
steps.body:
Start with a true rule: **If it's a dog, then it's a mammal.**

- **Converse** (swap): If it's a mammal, it's a dog. *False*: cats.
- **Inverse** (negate both): If it's not a dog, it's not a mammal. *False*: cats again.
- **Contrapositive** (swap *and* negate): If it's not a mammal, it's not a dog. *True!*

The contrapositive always agrees with the original. The converse and inverse don't, though they always agree with each other.

steps.prompt: Check the claim with a full table. Fill in all four versions of 'if P then Q'.
steps.hint: Each column is an if-then: it's false only when its own 'if' part is true and its 'then' part is false.
steps.explanation: Original and contrapositive are both **T, F, T, T**: identical in every row, so they're equivalent. Converse and inverse are both **T, T, F, T**: equivalent to each other, but they disagree with the original in two rows. That's why 'it's a mammal, so it's a dog' is a trap.

steps.prompt: Assume this rule is true: **'If Cleo is at the café, her bike is parked outside.'** Which statements are guaranteed to follow?

items.text: If Cleo's bike isn't outside, Cleo isn't at the café.
Cleo's bike is outside whenever she's at the café.
Cleo is never at the café without her bike outside.
If Cleo's bike is outside, Cleo is at the café.
If Cleo isn't at the café, her bike isn't outside.
Seeing Cleo's bike outside proves she's inside.

steps.hint: Turn each card into 'if ___ then ___' and compare it with the original: swapped? negated? both?
steps.explanation: The first card is the **contrapositive**, and the next two are rewordings of the original: all guaranteed. 'Bike outside, so Cleo's inside' is the **converse**, and 'Cleo's away, so no bike' is the **inverse**. Neither follows: she might have left her bike there and walked to the cinema.

steps.title: 'Only if' points the other way
steps.body:
'You can play chess here **only if** you book a table' means: **if** you play chess, **then** you booked a table.

**P only if Q** = **if P then Q**.

It does *not* promise that booking gets you a game. 'Only if' introduces the **requirement**, not the trigger. Compare: 'P **if** Q' = 'if Q then P', which points the opposite way.

steps.prompt: **'Ben comes to puzzle night only if Ana comes.'** Which statement says the same thing?
choices: If Ana comes, Ben comes
If Ben comes, Ana comes
Ben and Ana always come together
If Ana doesn't come, Ben might still come
steps.hint: Which person's attendance is the requirement? The 'only if' part is the 'then' part.
steps.explanation: P only if Q = if P then Q, with P = 'Ben comes' and Q = 'Ana comes'. Ana's presence is a requirement for Ben's. It doesn't guarantee Ben shows up (option 1 is the converse), and if Ana stays home, Ben definitely doesn't come (the contrapositive), which rules out the last option.

steps.prompt: Board-game night! Match each friend with a game and a snack. Two clues are if-thens: their contrapositives do the heavy lifting.
clues: If Ana is playing chess, then she's eating nachos.
Ben plays Uno only if he's eating cookies.
Ana is allergic to corn, so she's having no nachos and no popcorn.
The Uno player is eating nachos.
steps.hint: Start with Ana's snack. Then read clue 1 backwards: if she isn't eating nachos, what can't she be playing?
steps.explanation: Clue 3 leaves **Ana with the cookies**. Clue 1's contrapositive: no nachos → **Ana isn't playing chess**. Clue 2 says 'if Ben plays Uno, he's eating cookies'; the cookies are Ana's, so by the contrapositive **Ben isn't playing Uno**. Ana isn't on Uno either (the Uno player eats nachos), so **Cleo plays Uno** and eats the **nachos**. Ana isn't on chess, so **Ana plays Scrabble**, and **Ben plays chess with the popcorn**.

steps.prompt: An ad says: **'Every champion runner trains with SpeedSoles.'** Even if that's true, what's wrong with concluding 'Train with SpeedSoles and you'll be a champion'?
choices: Nothing: it's the contrapositive, so it's equivalent
It's the converse: the ad says champion → SpeedSoles, not SpeedSoles → champion
It's the inverse, which is always false
Ads can't be analysed with logic
steps.explanation: 'Every champion trains with SpeedSoles' = if champion, then SpeedSoles. Flipping it to 'if SpeedSoles, then champion' is the **converse**, which doesn't follow: thousands of ordinary runners might use them too. (The converse isn't *always* false, just not guaranteed.) The real contrapositive would be 'If you don't train with SpeedSoles, you're not a champion.'

lessons.title: Valid or invalid?
lessons.takeaway: An argument is valid when its conclusion can't be false while its premises are true; affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent fail that test.

steps.title: What 'valid' means
steps.body:
An **argument** is some premises plus a conclusion. It's **valid** if the conclusion **can't** be false when all the premises are true. Validity is about the **shape**, not the topic.

Two valid shapes you use every day:

- **Modus ponens**: If P then Q. P. So Q.
- **Modus tollens**: If P then Q. Not Q. So not P.

'If Dev's phone is dead, he can't reply. He replied. So his phone isn't dead.' That's modus tollens.

steps.title: Two invalid look-alikes
steps.body:
These look similar but are **invalid**:

- **Affirming the consequent**: If P then Q. Q. So P.
- **Denying the antecedent**: If P then Q. Not P. So not Q.

'If it rained, the street is wet. The street is wet. So it rained.' Maybe a street-cleaning truck went by. 'It didn't rain, so the street is dry'? Same problem. The rule only tells you what happens *when it rains*.

steps.prompt: Valid or invalid? Sort each argument by its shape.

items.text: If the alarm rings, Cleo wakes up. The alarm rang. So Cleo woke up.
If Dev's phone is dead, he can't reply. He replied. So his phone isn't dead.
If the oven is on, the kitchen is warm. The kitchen isn't warm. So the oven is off.
If you're a member, you get a discount. Ana is a member. So Ana gets a discount.
If it rained, the street is wet. The street is wet. So it rained.
If you're a member, you get a discount. Ana got a discount. So Ana is a member.
If it rained, the street is wet. It didn't rain. So the street is dry.
If Ben studied, he passed. Ben didn't study. So Ben failed.

steps.hint: Label the parts: P is the 'if' part, Q the 'then' part. Is the second premise P, not P, Q or not Q?
steps.explanation: **Valid:** the alarm and the member cards are modus ponens (P, so Q); the phone and the oven are modus tollens (not Q, so not P). **Invalid:** the wet street and Ana's discount *affirm the consequent* (Q, so P): there could be a happy-hour discount for everyone. The dry street and Ben *deny the antecedent* (not P, so not Q): Ben might have passed anyway.

steps.prompt: Test affirming the consequent with a table. An argument is valid only if **'premises → conclusion'** is true in **every** row. The premises are given; fill in the last column.
steps.hint: Use the given column: where the premises are false, the if-then is automatically true.
steps.explanation: The last column is **T, T, F, T**. The false row, P false and Q true, is a **counterexample**: both premises hold (street wet, and the rule is fine), yet the conclusion fails (it didn't rain). One counterexample row is enough to make an argument form invalid.

steps.prompt: Now modus tollens: **If P then Q. Not Q. So not P.** Fill in the last column.

columns.expr: ((P -> Q) and not Q) -> not P
columns.label: Premises → not P

steps.explanation: **T in every row**: no counterexample exists, so modus tollens is **valid**. The premises are only both true in the bottom row (P and Q both false), and there 'not P' is true. A formula that's true in every row is called a **tautology**.

steps.title: Valid isn't the same as true
steps.body:
Validity only checks the **shape**. An argument is **sound** if it's valid *and* all its premises are actually true. Only a sound argument guarantees its conclusion.

'All cats can fly. Tom is a cat. So Tom can fly.' **Valid** (perfect shape) but **unsound**: premise 1 is false.

And an invalid argument can land on a true conclusion by luck. It just doesn't *prove* it.

steps.prompt: **'All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. So penguins can fly.'** How would you rate this argument?
choices: Valid and sound
Valid but unsound
Invalid but sound
Invalid: it affirms the consequent
steps.explanation: The shape is fine: if every bird flies and penguins are birds, penguins would have to fly. So it's **valid**. But 'all birds can fly' is false (penguins, ostriches, kiwis), so it's **unsound**. 'Invalid but sound' is impossible: sound means valid with true premises.

steps.prompt: **'Every phone sold at this shop comes with a warranty. Ana's phone has a warranty. So Ana's phone was sold at this shop.'** What's going on?
choices: Valid: it's modus ponens
Valid: it's modus tollens
Invalid: it affirms the consequent
Invalid: it denies the antecedent
steps.hint: Rewrite 'Every phone sold here has a warranty' as 'If ___, then ___'.
steps.explanation: Rewrite as if-then: if sold here (P), then warranty (Q). The second premise says Q, and the conclusion is P: that's **affirming the consequent**. Plenty of other shops give warranties too.

steps.prompt: If-thens chain: if P then Q, and if Q then R, so if P then R. Dev's morning went wrong. Put the deduction in order, from the fact to the conclusion.
items: If the alarm doesn't ring, Dev oversleeps. So Dev overslept.
If Dev oversleeps, he misses the 8:10 bus. So he missed the bus.
If Dev misses the bus, he's late for work. So he was late.
If Dev is late, he misses the 9:00 meeting. So he missed the meeting.
steps.hint: Each step's 'if' part must already have been established by the step before.
steps.explanation: Each step is **modus ponens**: the previous conclusion triggers the next rule. Chaining if-thens like this is valid, but the chain is only as strong as its weakest rule: if Dev sometimes catches a later bus that still gets him in on time, the conclusion isn't guaranteed.

lessons.title: Necessary vs sufficient
lessons.takeaway: In 'if P then Q', P is sufficient for Q and Q is necessary for P; 'P unless Q' means 'if not Q, then P'.

steps.title: Two kinds of condition
steps.body:
In **if P then Q**:

- P is **sufficient** for Q: P on its own is enough to guarantee Q.
- Q is **necessary** for P: without Q, no P.

Being a dog is sufficient for being a mammal. Being a mammal is necessary for being a dog, but not enough.

Oxygen is necessary for a campfire, but not sufficient: you also need fuel and a spark.

steps.prompt: Sort each condition. Is the first part necessary, sufficient, or both, for the second?

items.text: Oxygen, for a campfire to burn
Being 18 or older, for voting in a US federal election
Knowing your PIN, for withdrawing cash at an ATM
Being a square, for being a rectangle
Rolling a 6, for rolling an even number on a die
Being someone's mother, for being a parent
Today being Saturday, for tomorrow being Sunday
Rolling a 2, 4 or 6, for rolling an even number on a die

steps.hint: Necessary: can the result happen without it? Sufficient: does it guarantee the result on its own?
steps.explanation: **Necessary only:** you can't vote under 18, but you also need to be a citizen; a PIN is useless without the card. **Sufficient only:** every square is a rectangle, but long thin rectangles aren't squares; a 6 is even, but so are 2 and 4. **Both:** the condition and the result always go together, which logic writes as **P if and only if Q**.

steps.title: Spotting the direction
steps.body:
These all mean **if P then Q**:

- 'P is **sufficient** for Q', 'P **guarantees** Q'
- 'Q is **necessary** for P', 'Q is **required** for P'
- 'P **only if** Q', '**no** P **without** Q'

And '**P if and only if Q**' means both directions: P is necessary *and* sufficient for Q.

steps.prompt: A job ad says: **'A degree is required for this role.'** Which conclusion is valid?
choices: Ana has a degree, so she'll be hired
Ben has no degree, so he won't be hired
Cleo wasn't hired, so she must not have a degree
Dev has two degrees, so he's the strongest candidate
steps.hint: Write the rule as 'if hired, then ___', then check each option's shape.
steps.explanation: 'Required' means necessary: if hired, then degree. Ben has no degree, so by **modus tollens** he won't be hired. Ana's degree is necessary but not sufficient (that's affirming the consequent). Cleo's case denies the antecedent: she might have a degree and lost out to someone else.

steps.title: Unless
steps.body:
'**P unless Q**' means **if not Q, then P**. 'You'll miss the bus unless you run' = if you don't run, you'll miss the bus.

Strictly, it says nothing about what happens if you *do* run: you might still miss it. In everyday talk, people often hear more ('if you run, you'll make it'), but the words alone don't promise that.

steps.prompt: Let M = 'you miss the bus' and R = 'you run'. Fill in 'M unless R' written as an if-then, and the simpler **M or R**. Do they match?
steps.hint: 'If not R, then M' is false only when not R is true (you didn't run) and M is false (you caught the bus).
steps.explanation: Both columns are **T, T, T, F**: identical, so **'P unless Q' is equivalent to 'P or Q'**: at least one of them happens. The only false row is 'you didn't run *and* you didn't miss the bus'. Running and still missing it (top row) doesn't break the statement.

steps.prompt: Cleo: **'I'll come to puzzle night unless it rains.'** It pours, and Cleo shows up anyway, dripping wet. Strictly speaking, did she break her word?
choices: Yes: 'unless it rains' means she won't come if it rains
No: she only promised to come if it *doesn't* rain
Yes: 'unless' means exactly one of the two happens
It can't be judged without knowing if she ran
steps.explanation: 'I'll come unless it rains' = if it doesn't rain, I'll come. Rain triggers nothing, so showing up in the rain keeps the statement true (it's the top row of the table you just filled in). Many people *hear* 'and if it rains I won't come', but that's an extra assumption.

units.title: Deduction in action
units.description: Quantifiers, logic grids and liars: put the tools to work.

lessons.title: All, some, none
lessons.takeaway: To deny 'all', one counterexample is enough; to deny 'some', you need 'none'; and examples alone never prove an 'all'.

steps.title: Quantifiers
steps.body:
**All**, **some** and **no** are quantifiers. In logic:

- **All** the cookies are gone: no exceptions.
- **Some** cookies are gone: *at least one* is, and maybe all of them.
- **No** cookies are gone: zero.

The surprise: 'some' doesn't mean 'not all'. If Ben ate every cookie, 'Ben ate some cookies' is still true, just weaker than what you could say.

steps.title: Negating all and some
steps.body:
To prove **'All the phones in the shop are on sale'** false, you don't need 'no phones are on sale'. **One** full-price phone is enough.

- not (all are) = **some are not**
- not (some are) = **none are**
- not (none are) = **some are**

steps.prompt: Claim: **'All the board games at the café are complete'** (no missing pieces). Which findings prove the claim false?

items.text: The chess set is missing a knight.
One of the Uno decks is missing a card.
Some of the games are missing pieces.
None of the games are complete.
The Scrabble set is complete.
Most of the games are complete.
Nobody has checked the jigsaws yet.
Three games were checked, and all three were complete.

steps.hint: What would you need to find to say 'Not all of them are complete'?
steps.explanation: A single incomplete game is a **counterexample**, so the knight, the Uno card, 'some are missing pieces' and 'none are complete' all sink the claim. Complete games, even many of them, are **consistent** with the claim but don't prove it, and unchecked jigsaws tell you nothing either way.

steps.prompt: What is the negation of **'Some of Dev's messages were rude'**?
choices: Some of Dev's messages were not rude
None of Dev's messages were rude
All of Dev's messages were rude
Most of Dev's messages were polite
steps.hint: A negation and the original can never both be true. Could 'some were rude' and 'some were not rude' both hold?
steps.explanation: not (some are) = **none are**. 'Some were not rude' isn't the negation: both statements can be true at once (a few rude messages, a few polite ones). A negation must be true exactly when the original is false.

steps.title: Chaining 'all'
steps.body:
'All' statements chain like if-thens: **All A are B** and **all B are C**, so **all A are C**.

But watch the middle. 'All cats are mammals' and 'all dogs are mammals' tell you **nothing** about cats and dogs. Draw circles: cats inside mammals, dogs inside mammals, and the two smaller circles never have to touch.

steps.prompt: Prove: **Every barista at the Puzzle Café can make a cappuccino.** Put the chain of 'all' statements in order.
items: Every barista at the Puzzle Café finished the café's training course.
Everyone who finished the training course passed the milk-steaming test.
Everyone who passed the milk-steaming test can make a cappuccino.
So every barista at the Puzzle Café can make a cappuccino.
steps.hint: Start with the baristas, and make each statement begin where the previous one ended.
steps.explanation: Each link's second group is the next link's first group: baristas → course → steaming test → cappuccino. That's two 'all' chains in a row, so the conclusion is **guaranteed**, as long as every link is true.

steps.prompt: **'All of Ana's friends love puzzles. Some puzzle lovers are night owls. So some of Ana's friends are night owls.'** Is this valid?
choices: Valid: the night owls are among the puzzle lovers, and so are Ana's friends
Invalid: the puzzle-loving night owls might all be people Ana doesn't know
Valid, but only if Ana herself is a night owl
Invalid: 'some' can never appear in a valid argument
steps.hint: Try to imagine a world where both premises are true but no friend of Ana's is a night owl.
steps.explanation: Draw it: Ana's friends sit inside the puzzle-lovers circle, and the night owls overlap the puzzle lovers *somewhere*, maybe in a part with none of Ana's friends. The conclusion *could* be true, but the premises don't force it, so it's **invalid**. 'Some' can appear in valid arguments: 'All A are B; some C are A; so some C are B' works.

steps.title: Deduction vs induction
steps.body:
**Deduction** goes from rules to a guaranteed conclusion, like everything so far. **Induction** generalizes from examples: 'Every swan I've seen is white, so all swans are white.'

Induction is how we learn from experience, but it's never guaranteed: Europeans believed all swans were white until they found black swans in Australia. No pile of examples **proves** an 'all', but **one counterexample** disproves it.

steps.prompt: Deduction (guaranteed, if the premises are true) or induction (a generalization from examples)?

items.text: All members get a free drink. Ana is a member. So Ana gets a free drink.
Every square is a rectangle, and this tile is square. So this tile is a rectangle.
If the café is closed, the lights are off. The lights are on. So the café isn't closed.
The café has opened at 8 every day this month, so it'll open at 8 tomorrow.
The last five times Ben said 'I'm 5 minutes away', he took 20. He'll be late again.
Every review I've read praises the cake, so most customers must like it.

steps.explanation: The first three apply rules (an 'all' statement, modus tollens) to reach conclusions that **can't** be false if the premises are true. The last three generalize from past cases: sensible bets, but a new case could break the pattern (a holiday closure, an on-time Ben, the reviews you didn't read).

lessons.title: Cracking logic grids
lessons.takeaway: Solve big puzzles by elimination: place what's certain, transfer every match across categories, and when stuck, test an assumption for a contradiction.

steps.title: The solver's toolkit
steps.body:
Bigger grids need a system:

- **Direct hits first**: a clue like 'Dev has the red mug' fills a cell and rules out the rest of its row and column.
- **Last one standing**: when a row or column has one possible cell left, it's a match.
- **Comparisons**: 'X arrived before Y' means X wasn't last and Y wasn't first.
- **Re-read**: a clue that was useless at the start can become decisive later.

steps.prompt: Four friends arrived at the café 15 minutes apart. Who arrived when?
clues: Ben arrived after Dev but before Ana.
Cleo wasn't the first to arrive.
Ana and Dev arrived exactly 30 minutes apart.
steps.hint: Who *can* be first? Clue 1 rules out two people, and clue 2 rules out one more.
steps.explanation: Clue 1 means Ben and Ana weren't first, and clue 2 rules out Cleo, so **Dev arrived at 6:00**. Clue 3 puts **Ana at 6:30**, 30 minutes after Dev. Ben is between them: **6:15**. That leaves **Cleo at 6:45**.

steps.prompt: Replay the deduction you just made. Put the steps in the order they have to happen.
items: Clue 1 (Dev, then Ben, then Ana) means neither Ben nor Ana was first.
Clue 2 rules out Cleo too, so Dev arrived first, at 6:00.
Clue 3: Ana came 30 minutes after Dev, so at 6:30.
Ben arrived between Dev and Ana, so at 6:15.
Only 6:45 is left, so that's Cleo.
steps.hint: Which fact can you establish with no other facts? Then what does that unlock?
steps.explanation: Each step needs the one before it: you can't place Ana with clue 3 until you know Dev's time, and Ben's slot depends on both. A good deduction is a chain where every link uses only what's already settled.

steps.title: Three categories
steps.body:
With three categories, every match links **three** things. If you learn 'Ana drinks tea' and 'the tea drinker plays chess', you've also learned **Ana plays chess**.

So whenever you settle a match or rule one out, **transfer it** to every sub-grid it touches. Most people get stuck on three-category grids because they forget this step, not because a clue is missing.

steps.prompt: The full Friday crew: four friends, four drinks, four games. Match everything.
clues: The latte drinker is playing Uno.
Ana is playing either chess or Jenga.
Ana is drinking a latte or a tea.
If Ana is playing Jenga, then she's drinking the latte.
Ben is playing chess or Jenga.
Dev is drinking tea or cocoa.
steps.hint: Combine clues 1 and 2: can Ana be the latte drinker? Then use clue 4 backwards.
steps.explanation: Clue 2 says Ana isn't on Uno, so by clue 1 she isn't the latte drinker: **Ana drinks tea** (clue 3). Clue 4's contrapositive: no latte → no Jenga, so **Ana plays chess**, and **Ben plays Jenga** (clue 5). Tea is taken, so **Dev drinks cocoa** (clue 6). Ben plays Jenga, not Uno, so he isn't the latte drinker: **Ben drinks lemonade**, and **Cleo drinks the latte and plays Uno**. That leaves **Dev with Scrabble**.

steps.prompt: Stuck on a grid, a solver assumes **'Ben sits at table 1'** and follows the clues. A few steps later, they need two people at table 3. What can they conclude?
choices: Ben doesn't sit at table 1
Ben sits at table 3
The puzzle has no solution
Nothing: assumptions aren't allowed in logic
steps.explanation: This is **proof by contradiction**: if an assumption leads to something impossible, the assumption is false. Cross out Ben–table 1 and carry on. It's a legitimate move, not a guess, because you only keep what the contradiction proves. (Option 3 would only follow if *every* option for Ben failed.)

lessons.title: Knights and knaves
lessons.takeaway: If someone who always lies or always tells the truth says S, then they're a truth-teller exactly when S is true: test each case and keep the one without a contradiction.

steps.title: The island
steps.body:
On the Island of Knights and Knaves, **knights always tell the truth** and **knaves always lie**. You can't tell them apart by looks, only by what they say.

The key move: if an islander says S, then **they're a knight exactly when S is true**. A knight's statements are all true; a knave's are all false. So test each possibility and throw out the ones that contradict themselves.

steps.prompt: An islander walks up and says: **'I am a knave.'** What follows?
choices: They're a knight
They're a knave
No islander could say that
They could be either
steps.hint: Try both cases. Suppose they're a knight: is the sentence true? Now suppose they're a knave.
steps.explanation: A knight would be lying by saying it, and knights don't lie. A knave would be telling the truth, and knaves can't. Either way it's a contradiction, so **no islander can say it**. (Saying 'I am a knight' is the opposite problem: anyone can say it, so it tells you nothing.)

steps.prompt: Ana says: **'Ben and I are both knaves.'** Put the reasoning in order to find out what they are.
items: Then her statement is true, so Ana is a knave: a contradiction.
So Ana is a knave, and her statement is false.
'Both knaves' is false, and Ana is a knave, so Ben must be a knight.
steps.explanation: Assume, find the contradiction, then use what's left: **Ana is a knave, Ben is a knight**. Check it: a knave saying the false sentence 'we're both knaves' (Ben is actually a knight) is perfectly consistent.

steps.prompt: Ben says: **'At least one of us (Ben or Cleo) is a knave.'** Let B = 'Ben is a knight' and C = 'Cleo is a knight'. Ben's claim is given. A row is possible only if B and Ben's claim match: fill in **B ↔ claim**.

columns.label: Ben's claim: not B OR not C

steps.hint: ↔ is true when both sides have the same value. Compare the B column with the claim column, row by row.
steps.explanation: Only the second row, **B true, C false**, is possible. If Ben were a knave (bottom rows), his claim would be true, and knaves can't say true things. If both were knights (top row), the claim would be false. So **Ben is a knight and Cleo is a knave**.

steps.title: Three islanders
steps.body:
Bigger puzzle. **Ana** says: 'Ben is a knave.' **Ben** says: 'Ana and Cleo are the same type.' Cleo stays silent.

Each speaker gives a condition:

- Ana's: **A ↔ not B** (Ana is a knight exactly when Ben is a knave)
- Ben's: **B ↔ (A ↔ C)** (Ben is a knight exactly when Ana and Cleo match)

A row of the table is a possible world only if **both** conditions are true.

steps.prompt: Fill in Ben's condition and the 'both' column. A = Ana is a knight, B = Ben is a knight, C = Cleo is a knight.
steps.hint: Work out A ↔ C first for each row, then compare it with B.
steps.explanation: The 'both' column is true in exactly **two** rows: (A knight, B knave, C knave) and (A knave, B knight, C knave). Ana and Ben swap roles between them, but **Cleo is a knave in both**.

steps.prompt: How many of the 8 rows are possible worlds?
steps.explanation: Two rows survive: A=T, B=F, C=F and A=F, B=T, C=F. Ana's condition already rules out half the table (Ana and Ben must be different types), and Ben's condition then forces Cleo's type in each remaining case.

steps.prompt: So what can you say for certain?
choices: Cleo is a knave, but Ana and Ben could be either way round
Ana is a knight and Ben is a knave
Cleo is a knight
Nothing: the puzzle has two answers, so it's broken
steps.explanation: Two possible worlds remain, and they disagree about Ana and Ben, so neither is determined. But they agree on Cleo: she's a **knave** in both. A puzzle can pin down exactly what it asks for even when other details stay open.
